title: Taxes, Regulation and Building Your Plan

submodules.title: 1. Why Taxes and Costs Matter
submodules.intro: Is the profit you see the profit you keep?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: WHY TAXES AND COSTS MATTER
The profit shown on a screen is a gross number. What you actually keep is the net number, after charges and taxes. Smart investors think in net terms from the start, because costs and taxes quietly take a slice of every result. Tax rules change often, so rates here are as of late 2026 and you should always check the latest rules or ask a qualified tax professional. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Securities Transaction Tax (STT) is charged on many trades even when the trade ends in a loss.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: GROSS VERSUS NET
• Gross return: the result before costs and taxes.
• Net return = gross return - costs - taxes.
• Two people with the same gross return can keep very different amounts.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE MAIN LEAKS
• Brokerage and other charges on each trade.
• STT, a small tax on the value of many trades.
• Fund expense ratios, which you met in Module 9.
• Capital gains tax when you sell at a profit.
• Tax on dividends and interest.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE HABIT TO BUILD
• Before any trade, ask what the net result would be after charges and tax.
• Fewer trades usually means lower costs and simpler taxes.
• Keep records of every trade, because you or your family will need them at tax time.

🍕 MINI CASE: GROSS TO NET
In her fictional simulator story, Meera makes a headline gain of ₹20,000. Charges take ₹2,000, so the gain left is ₹18,000. Short-term capital gains tax at 20% takes 0.20 x 18,000 = ₹3,600. Her net result is 20,000 - 2,000 - 3,600 = ₹14,400, which is 72% of the headline figure. Aarav had only looked at the ₹20,000.

🧪 TRY IT: FIND THE NET
A fictional trade has a gross gain of ₹10,000 and charges of ₹1,000. Short-term capital gains tax of 20% applies to the ₹9,000 left. What is the net result?
(Answer: tax = 0.20 x 9,000 = ₹1,800. Net = 10,000 - 1,000 - 1,800 = ₹7,200.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Think in net returns, after charges and tax. Keep records, trade less and always check the latest rules.

quiz.question: What is net return?
options: Gross return minus costs and taxes
quiz.explanation: Net return is what is left after costs and taxes.

quiz.explanation: Charges and taxes both come out of your gain.

options: No, they change, so check the latest rules
quiz.explanation: Budgets and laws can change rates and rules.

submodules.title: 2. Capital Gains: Short-Term and Long-Term
submodules.intro: Does it matter how long you hold a share before selling?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: CAPITAL GAINS: SHORT-TERM AND LONG-TERM
A capital gain is the profit when you sell an asset for more than you paid. In India, the tax depends on how long you held it. For listed shares and equity mutual funds, holding for more than 12 months counts as long-term, and long-term gains get a lower rate. Tax rules change often, so rates here are as of late 2026 and you should always check the latest rules or ask a qualified tax professional. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Gains up to ₹1.25 lakh a year from long-term equity are currently exempt from tax.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE RULES FOR LISTED EQUITY (LATE 2026)
• Held for 12 months or less: short-term capital gain (STCG), taxed at 20%.
• Held for more than 12 months: long-term capital gain (LTCG), taxed at 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh in a financial year.
• These rates exclude surcharge and cess, which can add a little more.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HOW TO CALCULATE
• Gain = selling price - buying price.
• STCG tax = gain x 20%.
• LTCG tax = (total long-term gain - ₹1,25,000) x 12.5%, if the gain is above ₹1,25,000.
• The tax is due on gains you have realised, which means you sold.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT THIS TEACHES
• Holding a little longer can cut the tax rate a lot.
• Do not let tax alone drive a decision. A bad investment is still bad after a tax saving.
• Budgets can change these numbers, so check each year.

🍕 MINI CASE: TWO HOLDING PERIODS
A fictional investor buys shares for ₹1,00,000 and sells them 8 months later for ₹1,30,000. The gain is ₹30,000, short-term, so the tax is 0.20 x 30,000 = ₹6,000. Another investor holds for 14 months and makes a gain of ₹1,50,000. The taxable part is 1,50,000 - 1,25,000 = ₹25,000, so the tax is 0.125 x 25,000 = ₹3,125.

🧪 TRY IT: TAX THE GAIN
A fictional investor has a long-term equity gain of ₹2,25,000 in one year. What is the tax? Then, what is the tax on a long-term gain of ₹1,00,000?
(Answer: for ₹2,25,000, the taxable part is 2,25,000 - 1,25,000 = ₹1,00,000, so tax = 0.125 x 1,00,000 = ₹12,500. For ₹1,00,000, the gain is below the exemption, so the tax is ₹0.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
For listed shares, holding more than 12 months gives a lower long-term rate and an annual exemption. Check each year's rules and do not let tax drive a bad decision.

quiz.explanation: Held for more than 12 months counts as long-term.

quiz.explanation: The gain is below the exemption, so no tax.

submodules.title: 3. Dividends, Interest and Other Income
submodules.intro: Is all investment income taxed the same way?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: DIVIDENDS, INTEREST AND OTHER INCOME
Not all investment income is taxed like capital gains. Dividends from shares and interest from bank deposits are generally added to your income and taxed at your slab rate. Gains from most debt mutual funds are also taxed at slab rate. Knowing the type of income helps you compare options fairly. Tax rules change often, so rates here are as of late 2026 and you should always check the latest rules or ask a qualified tax professional. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Two investments with the same 7% return can leave you with different amounts, because of how each is taxed.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: SLAB RATE
• Your slab rate is the tax rate that applies to your income level.
• Dividends and bank interest are added to your income and taxed at that rate.
• Slab rates differ by person, so the same dividend can be taxed differently for different people.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: DIFFERENT INVESTMENTS, DIFFERENT TAX
• Listed shares and equity funds: capital gains rules, plus tax on dividends.
• Bank fixed deposits: interest taxed at slab rate, and the bank may deduct TDS.
• Most debt mutual funds: gains taxed at slab rate.
• Always compare returns after tax, not before.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: TDS
• TDS means tax deducted at source. The payer deducts some tax before paying you.
• It is not an extra tax. It counts towards your tax bill, and any excess can be claimed back by filing a return.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE SAME DIVIDEND, TWO TAX BILLS
A fictional dividend of ₹10,000 is paid. For someone in a 10% slab, the tax is 0.10 x 10,000 = ₹1,000, so they keep ₹9,000. For someone in a 30% slab, the tax is 0.30 x 10,000 = ₹3,000, so they keep ₹7,000. Meera notes that comparing investments means comparing what each person keeps after tax.

🧪 TRY IT: KEEP WHAT AFTER TAX
A fictional fixed deposit pays ₹8,000 interest in a year. For someone in a 20% slab, what is the tax and what is kept?
(Answer: tax = 0.20 x 8,000 = ₹1,600. Kept = 8,000 - 1,600 = ₹6,400.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Different incomes are taxed in different ways. Compare returns after tax, and understand what TDS is.

quiz.question: How are dividends and bank interest generally taxed?
quiz.explanation: They are added to your income and taxed at your slab rate.

quiz.question: A ₹10,000 dividend is taxed at a 30% slab. What is the tax?

quiz.explanation: Tax treatment changes the amount you actually keep.

submodules.title: 4. Setting Off Losses
submodules.intro: Can a loss on one share reduce the tax on another?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: SETTING OFF LOSSES
Losses are not only painful. They can also reduce your tax. In India, capital losses can be set off against capital gains in the same year, and some can be carried forward. Knowing the rules helps you plan, but it never makes a loss a good thing. Tax rules change often, so rates here are as of late 2026 and you should always check the latest rules or ask a qualified tax professional. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Currently, an unused capital loss can be carried forward for up to 8 years, but only if the return is filed on time.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: SET-OFF RULES (LATE 2026)
• Short-term capital loss can be set off against both short-term and long-term gains.
• Long-term capital loss can be set off only against long-term gains.
• Capital losses cannot be set off against salary or other regular income.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: CARRY FORWARD
• Losses that cannot be fully used this year can be carried forward to future years.
• To keep the right to carry forward, the return must be filed on time.
• Keep clear records of every loss.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: A CAUTION
• Do not sell a good investment just to book a loss for tax.
• A tax saving is small next to a lost opportunity.
• Ask a parent or a qualified professional when real tax filing is involved.

🍕 MINI CASE: NETTING A LOSS
A fictional investor has a short-term gain of ₹30,000 and a short-term loss of ₹12,000 in the same year. The net short-term gain is 30,000 - 12,000 = ₹18,000, and the tax at 20% is 0.20 x 18,000 = ₹3,600, instead of ₹6,000 without the loss. Aarav asks if he can use a long-term loss against a short-term gain. Meera says no, because a long-term loss can only reduce long-term gains.

🧪 TRY IT: CAN IT BE SET OFF
A fictional investor has a long-term capital loss of ₹10,000 and a short-term capital gain of ₹10,000. Can the loss be set off against the gain? What is the tax on the short-term gain at 20%?
(Answer: no, a long-term loss can be set off only against long-term gains. The tax on the short-term gain is 0.20 x 10,000 = ₹2,000.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Capital losses can reduce capital gains tax under set-off rules, and some can be carried forward if returns are filed on time. Never keep or sell an investment only for tax reasons.

quiz.explanation: Short-term losses can reduce either kind of gain.

quiz.explanation: Long-term losses can only reduce long-term gains.

quiz.question: Why should you not sell a good investment only to book a loss?
options: A small tax saving can cost you a bigger lost opportunity
quiz.explanation: Tax should not outweigh the investment merits.

submodules.title: 5. Trading Costs and Charges
submodules.intro: What does each trade really cost?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: TRADING COSTS AND CHARGES
Every trade has costs beyond the share price. Some are small, but they repeat with each trade, and they apply even when you lose. Knowing them helps you see why frequent trading is harder than it looks. Tax rules change often, so rates here are as of late 2026 and you should always check the latest rules or ask a qualified tax professional. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A buy-and-sell round trip needs the price to rise a little just to cover the charges before you make any profit.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE CHARGES
• Brokerage: the broker's fee, which varies by broker.
• STT (Securities Transaction Tax): a government tax on trades.
• Exchange and SEBI charges, GST on certain fees and stamp duty on purchases.
• Demat charges, such as a fee when shares are sold.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: STT RATES (AS OF 2026)
• Equity delivery: 0.1% on both the buy and the sell.
• Equity intraday: 0.025% on the sell side only.
• Futures: 0.05% on the sell side, raised from 0.02% from 1 April 2026.
• Options: 0.15% on the premium when sold, raised from 0.10% from 1 April 2026.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: BREAKEVEN FROM COSTS
• Break-even % = total round-trip charges ÷ amount invested x 100.
• The higher the break-even, the harder it is to profit from small moves.
• Costs are certain, while profits are not.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE ROUND TRIP
Meera's fictional delivery trade buys shares worth ₹50,000 and sells them for ₹55,000. STT on the buy is 0.1% x 50,000 = ₹50, and on the sell is 0.1% x 55,000 = ₹55, a total of ₹105. Say other charges bring the total round-trip cost to ₹300. The break-even is 300 ÷ 50,000 x 100 = 0.6%, so the price must rise 0.6% just to cover costs.

🧪 TRY IT: CALCULATE THE STT
A fictional trader sells an intraday position worth ₹1,00,000. What is the STT at 0.025%? Another trader sells a futures position worth ₹2,00,000. What is the STT at 0.05%?
(Answer: intraday STT = 0.025% x 1,00,000 = ₹25. Futures STT = 0.05% x 2,00,000 = ₹100.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Charges repeat with every trade and apply even to losing trades. Know the costs, since they set a break-even that the price must clear first.

quiz.question: What is STT?
quiz.explanation: Securities Transaction Tax is charged on many trades.

submodules.title: 6. Investor or Trader: How Tax Differs
submodules.intro: Is tax on a long-term investor the same as on an active trader?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: INVESTOR OR TRADER: HOW TAX DIFFERS
The tax system treats long-term investors and active traders differently. Share investments are usually taxed as capital gains. Income from futures and options is generally treated as business income. Derivatives are only for adults, and this lesson is for understanding, not for trading. Tax rules change often, so rates here are as of late 2026 and you should always check the latest rules or ask a qualified tax professional. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Even though F&O profit is business income, you cannot use F&O losses to cancel capital gains from delivery trades, because they are taxed in separate baskets.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: INVESTORS
• Delivery-based share and fund investments are taxed as capital gains.
• Holding period decides short-term or long-term treatment.
• Many small investors only need simple capital gains reports.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: TRADERS
• Futures and options income is generally treated as non-speculative business income, taxed at slab rate.
• Intraday equity trading is generally treated as speculative business income.
• Business losses may be carried forward under certain rules, if returns are filed on time.
• Traders often need a more detailed return and a qualified tax professional.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHY IT MATTERS
• Active trading adds tax paperwork as well as costs.
• Tax liability can arise even in a year with a poor overall result, depending on how gains and losses are classified.
• For learners, the best practice is a simulator, and a parent or guardian should be part of any real step.

🍕 MINI CASE: TWO YEARS OF F&O
A fictional adult trader loses ₹60,000 in F&O in year one. In year two, the net F&O profit is ₹1,00,000. Under the carry-forward rule, the loss can be set off, if returns were filed on time, leaving 1,00,000 - 60,000 = ₹40,000 taxable. At a hypothetical slab rate of 20%, the tax is 0.20 x 40,000 = ₹8,000. Without the carry-forward, the tax would have been 0.20 x 1,00,000 = ₹20,000. Meera notes that this is a lot of paperwork for something so risky.

🧪 TRY IT: COMPARE THE TWO
A fictional adult has a net F&O profit of ₹1,50,000 and a hypothetical slab rate of 20%. What is the tax? How is that different from the way a delivery investor with a long-term gain of ₹1,50,000 is taxed?
(Answer: F&O tax = 0.20 x 1,50,000 = ₹30,000 at the hypothetical slab rate. The investor's LTCG tax is 0.125 x (1,50,000 - 1,25,000) = ₹3,125, because of the lower long-term rate and exemption.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Investors and traders are taxed differently. Active trading adds paperwork and cost on top of risk, so keep derivatives to a simulator until you are an adult.

submodules.title: 7. Minors, Parents and Clubbing of Income
submodules.intro: What are the rules when the investor is under 18?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: MINORS, PARENTS AND CLUBBING OF INCOME
In India, a minor cannot trade independently. A parent or legal guardian opens and operates any account on the minor's behalf, and the minor's investment income is generally added to a parent's income for tax. This lesson explains the rules so you can talk about them with your family. Tax rules change often, so rates here are as of late 2026 and you should always check the latest rules or ask a qualified tax professional. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A minor demat account is not a way to avoid tax, because income from it is generally added to the higher-earning parent's income.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: MINOR DEMAT ACCOUNTS
• Opened in the child's name, but operated by a parent or legal guardian until the child turns 18.
• The child needs a PAN, and the guardian completes the paperwork.
• Intraday trading and F&O are generally not allowed in a minor's account.
• At 18, the account is converted to a normal one after the required formalities.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: CLUBBING OF INCOME
• Income from a minor's investments, such as dividends and capital gains, is generally added to the income of the parent with the higher income.
• A small exemption per child may apply, so check the current rules.
• Income a child earns from their own talent or skill, like acting or sport, is generally treated differently.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT YOU CAN DO NOW
• Practise on the Bull Run simulator, which uses no real money.
• Talk to your parents or guardians about goals and savings.
• Learn the rules now, so you are ready at 18.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE CHILD'S DIVIDEND
A fictional child's demat account, run by a parent, receives a dividend of ₹10,000. This is added to the income of the parent who earns more. If that parent's slab rate is 30%, the tax is about 0.30 x 10,000 = ₹3,000, before any small exemption. Aarav says it is the child's money, so it should be tax-free. Meera explains that the clubbing rule treats it differently.

🧪 TRY IT: WHO PAYS
A fictional minor's account earns a capital gain of ₹20,000 that is clubbed with a parent in a 20% slab. Roughly how much tax does the parent pay, before any exemption, and who operates the account?
(Answer: roughly 0.20 x 20,000 = ₹4,000. The parent or legal guardian operates the account until the child turns 18.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
A minor's account is operated by a parent or guardian, and its income is generally taxed in the higher-earning parent's hands. Learn now, and practise on a simulator.

submodules.title: 8. Who Regulates the Market?
submodules.intro: Who makes sure the market plays by the rules?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: WHO REGULATES THE MARKET?
Markets need referees. In India, several bodies have different jobs, and knowing who does what tells you where to look for rules, registration and help. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
SEBI was set up in 1988 and was given legal powers by the SEBI Act of 1992.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE MAIN BODIES
• SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India): regulates securities markets, brokers, mutual funds and advisers, and protects investors.
• RBI (Reserve Bank of India): the central bank, which regulates banks and money matters.
• IRDAI regulates insurance. PFRDA regulates pensions.
• Exchanges (NSE and BSE) run the trading platforms.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE PLUMBING
• Depositories (NSDL and CDSL) hold shares in electronic form.
• Clearing corporations make sure trades are settled.
• AMFI is the industry body for mutual funds.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: REGISTRATION CHECK
• Brokers, advisers and research analysts must be registered with SEBI to offer their services.
• SEBI's website has a list of registered intermediaries.
• If someone is not registered but gives paid investment advice, treat that as a warning sign.

🍕 MINI CASE: CHECKING A BROKER
Meera's fictional family wants to open an account and she asks who is allowed to run it. She learns the broker must be SEBI-registered, the shares will sit with a depository like NSDL or CDSL, and trades will happen on NSE or BSE. When a stranger in a chat group offers 'guaranteed' tips for a fee, she checks SEBI's list and finds no entry. She stays away.

🧪 TRY IT: MATCH THE JOB
Which body does each job? (a) regulates banks, (b) regulates the securities market and protects investors, (c) holds shares electronically, (d) runs the trading platform.
(Answer: (a) RBI, (b) SEBI, (c) a depository such as NSDL or CDSL, (d) an exchange such as NSE or BSE.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Different bodies regulate banks, markets, insurance and pensions. Always check whether an adviser or broker is SEBI-registered.

quiz.explanation: SEBI regulates securities markets and protects investors.

submodules.title: 9. Your Rights and Safety Nets
submodules.intro: What can you do if something goes wrong?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: YOUR RIGHTS AND SAFETY NETS
Investors have rights, and the system has safety nets. Knowing them in advance makes you harder to fool and quicker to act. A parent or guardian should always be involved in real accounts. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
SEBI runs an online complaint system called SCORES, and it also supports an online dispute resolution process for investor complaints.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: YOUR BASIC RIGHTS
• To receive contract notes and statements for your trades.
• To be given clear information about charges and risks.
• To make a complaint and have it looked at.
• To nominate someone to receive your investments if something happens to you.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: IF THERE IS A PROBLEM
• First, write to the broker or company and keep a copy.
• If it is not solved, escalate through SEBI's complaint system (SCORES) or the online dispute resolution process.
• Keep contract notes, statements, emails and screenshots as evidence.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: STAYING SAFE
• Check your statements every month.
• Turn on two-factor login and never share OTPs or passwords.
• Be careful about giving anyone power of attorney over your account.
• Use only registered intermediaries and official apps.

🍕 MINI CASE: CHECKING THE CONTRACT NOTE
In a fictional story, Aarav's parent checks a contract note showing 100 shares bought at ₹250, but the order was placed at ₹245. The difference is (250 - 245) x 100 = ₹500. They write to the broker with the order screenshot, and the broker replies. Because they kept records, the issue is solved. Had it not been, they could escalate through SEBI's complaint system.

🧪 TRY IT: WHAT WOULD YOU DO
A fictional message says, 'Your demat account is blocked. Share your OTP now to unblock it.' What should you do, and who should you tell?
(Answer: never share the OTP. Do not click any links. Contact your broker only through their official app or website, and tell a parent or guardian straight away.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Keep records, check statements, protect OTPs and know the steps for a complaint. Registration and good habits are your best safety nets.

options: Never share it and tell a parent or guardian
quiz.explanation: OTPs must never be shared.

quiz.question: Why keep contract notes and statements?
options: They are evidence if there is a dispute
quiz.explanation: Records support any complaint.

submodules.title: 10. Market Rules and Unfair Practices
submodules.intro: What is allowed in the market, and what is not?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: MARKET RULES AND UNFAIR PRACTICES
Markets have rules about how trades settle and about fair play. Some actions are illegal, such as trading on secret information. Knowing the basics keeps you safe and shows why regulators exist. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A trade in the Indian cash market usually settles in one working day, a system called T+1.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HOW TRADING WORKS
• Normal trading hours are 9:15 am to 3:30 pm, after a pre-open session from 9:00 to 9:15.
• T+1 settlement: shares bought on a Monday normally reach your demat on the next working day.
• Many shares have daily price bands that limit how far the price can move in one day.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: UNFAIR PRACTICES
• Insider trading: trading on important information that is not yet public, such as unreleased results. It is illegal.
• Price manipulation: creating false activity to move a price, such as pump and dump.
• Front running: trading ahead of a large order that you know about.
• SEBI can impose penalties and bans for such practices.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT TO REMEMBER
• If you receive information that feels secret, do not trade on it and do not pass it on.
• If a deal depends on rushing and secrecy, it is a red flag.
• Honest research from public sources is always fine.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE SECRET RESULTS
In a fictional story, a company employee knows that results due next week will be very strong. If he buys shares before the news is public, that is insider trading. A friend who hears it and buys can also be in trouble. Meera only trades on public information. Another example: a share at ₹200 with a 10% daily band can move between 200 - 20 = ₹180 and 200 + 20 = ₹220 that day.

🧪 TRY IT: FIND THE BAND
A fictional share closes at ₹500 and has a 20% daily price band. What is the range for the next day? What does insider trading mean?
(Answer: the range is 500 - 100 = ₹400 to 500 + 100 = ₹600. Insider trading means trading on important non-public information, which is illegal.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Settlement rules, price bands and fair-play laws protect the market. Never trade on secret information, and avoid anything built on pressure and secrecy.

quiz.question: What is insider trading?
quiz.explanation: It uses secret information that can move a price.

quiz.question: What does T+1 settlement mean?
options: A trade settles one working day later
A trade settles in a year
quiz.explanation: Cash market trades usually settle on the next working day.

quiz.question: A share at ₹200 has a 10% daily band. What is the lower limit?
A share closes at ₹500 with a 20% band. What is the upper limit?
What should you do if you receive secret information about a company?
options: Do not trade on it or pass it on
quiz.explanation: Trading on secrets is illegal.

submodules.title: 11. Goals, Inflation and Time Horizons
submodules.intro: How do you decide what to save for and how to invest it?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: GOALS, INFLATION AND TIME HORIZONS
Good plans start with goals, not with shares. Each goal has an amount, a date and a different tolerance for risk. Inflation also raises the cost of future goals, so what costs a rupee today will cost more later. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
The Rule of 72 gives a quick estimate: divide 72 by the yearly return to find about how many years it takes money to double.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: GOALS AND TIME HORIZONS
• Short term (under 3 years): keep money safe in savings or low-risk options, not in shares.
• Medium term (3 to 7 years): a mix.
• Long term (7 years or more): more room for equity, because there is time to recover from falls.
• These are common guidelines, not fixed rules.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: INFLATION
• Future cost = today's cost x (1 + inflation) raised to the number of years.
• Plan goals in future money, not in today's money.
• Money that earns less than inflation loses buying power.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE SAFETY LAYER
• Emergency fund first: often 3 to 6 months of expenses, kept safe and easy to reach.
• Insurance questions belong with parents or guardians.
• Only invest money you will not need soon.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE COLLEGE COST
Meera's fictional goal is a course that costs ₹1,00,000 today. With inflation at 6% a year, in 10 years it will cost about 1,00,000 x 1.06 to the power of 10, roughly ₹1,79,085. A laptop she wants in 1 year, costing ₹60,000, should not be in shares because the time is too short. Rule of 72: at 8% a year, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years.

🧪 TRY IT: ESTIMATE THE DOUBLING
Using the Rule of 72, about how many years does money take to double at 12% a year? What does the monthly expenses of ₹30,000 mean for a 6-month emergency fund?
(Answer: 72 ÷ 12 = 6 years. A 6-month emergency fund is 6 x 30,000 = ₹1,80,000.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Start with goals, dates and inflation, then match each goal to the right level of risk. Build an emergency fund first.

quiz.question: Where should money needed within 1 year usually be kept?
quiz.explanation: Short goals cannot wait out market falls.

quiz.question: Using the Rule of 72, how long does money take to double at 8% a year?
quiz.explanation: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years.

quiz.question: A cost of ₹1,00,000 grows with 6% inflation for 10 years. About what is it then?
quiz.explanation: 1,00,000 x 1.06 to the power of 10 is about ₹1,79,085.

quiz.question: Monthly expenses are ₹30,000. What is a 6-month emergency fund?
What is true about inflation?
options: It raises the cost of future goals
quiz.explanation: Inflation makes future goals cost more.

submodules.title: 12. Your Complete Investing Plan
submodules.intro: Can you pull the whole journey into one page you can follow?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: YOUR COMPLETE INVESTING PLAN
You have travelled from saving and spending to markets, analysis, risk, psychology, tax and rules. This final lesson puts everything on one page: a plan you can write, share with a parent or guardian, and review. A plan does not guarantee profit. It guards you against your own worst moments. Tax rules change often, so rates here are as of late 2026 and you should always check the latest rules or ask a qualified tax professional. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A short written plan that you actually follow often beats a clever plan that lives only in your head.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE ONE-PAGE PLAN
1. Goals: what, how much, and by when?
2. Safety first: emergency fund and insurance, discussed with a parent or guardian.
3. Asset allocation: your split between equity, debt, gold and cash.
4. Instruments: for example low-cost index funds and a regular SIP.
5. Costs and tax: expected net returns after charges and tax.
6. Risk rules: maximum risk per idea and maximum size per holding.
7. Behaviour rules: waiting period, checklist and journal.
8. Review: dates to check progress and rebalance.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: PATIENT VERSUS BUSY
• Long holding periods mean lower tax rates and fewer charges.
• Low-cost funds keep more of the return with you.
• Frequent trading adds charges, higher short-term tax and more emotional mistakes.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: BEFORE ANY REAL MONEY
• Practise on the simulator first.
• Involve a parent or guardian, because accounts for minors are operated by them.
• Use only SEBI-registered intermediaries and official apps.
• Check the latest tax rules, or ask a qualified professional.

🍕 MINI CASE: TWO STYLES, ONE YEAR
Both Meera and Aarav make a fictional 10% gross gain on ₹1,00,000, which is ₹10,000. Meera holds an index fund for over 12 months. The fund cost is ₹500 and her gain is within the ₹1.25 lakh exemption, so tax is ₹0 and she keeps ₹9,500. Aarav trades actively. Trading charges are ₹3,000, and short-term tax at 20% on the remaining ₹7,000 is ₹1,400, so he keeps 10,000 - 3,000 - 1,400 = ₹5,600 (simplified). Same market, very different results.

🧪 TRY IT: BUILD YOUR OWN
Write your one-page plan using the eight lines above for a simulator account. Then compute the net result for a fictional ₹1,00,000 held over 12 months with a gross gain of ₹12,000, fund costs of ₹600 and no tax because the gain is within the exemption.
(Answer: net = 12,000 - 600 = ₹11,400, which is 11.4% on ₹1,00,000. Share your plan with a parent, teacher or guardian and review it every few months.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
A written plan ties goals, risk, costs, tax, behaviour and review together. No plan guarantees profit, so practise on a simulator, check the latest rules and involve a parent or guardian in every real money decision. Congratulations on finishing the Bull Run modules!

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the one-page plan?
options: To tie goals, risk, costs, tax and behaviour rules into one routine
quiz.explanation: A plan keeps your choices consistent.

quiz.question: A gross gain is ₹10,000, fund cost is ₹500 and there is no tax. What is the net?
Which style usually costs less in charges and tax?
options: Holding low-cost funds for the long term
quiz.explanation: Long holding and low costs keep more of your return.

quiz.question: A gross gain is ₹12,000 and cost is ₹600 with no tax. What is the net percentage on ₹1,00,000?
Does any plan guarantee profit?
options: No, risk remains, so practise on a simulator and involve a parent or guardian
quiz.explanation: No plan removes risk.
